name: 1969 March Storm

phenomena.details: Major geomagnetic storm with Dst ~ −429 nT during the maximum of Solar Cycle 20.

impacts.description: HF radio communications severely disrupted; polar radio routes experienced extended blackouts.
Aurora visible at mid-latitudes across North America and Europe; widely reported by the public.
GIC effects detected in long transmission lines and pipelines across North America.

papers.title: Geomagnetic activity during the March 1969 storm period
papers.authors: Caan, M. N., McPherron, R. L., Russell, C. T.
papers.keyFinding: Analyzed the March 1969 storm as a significant event in the emerging satellite era, with enhanced in-situ solar wind data providing improved understanding of storm drivers.

summary: The March 1969 geomagnetic storm (Dst ~ −429 nT) was a major event during Solar Cycle 20 maximum, causing widespread HF radio blackouts and aurora at mid-latitudes, studied with early satellite-era instrumentation.
description: On March 8, 1969, during the maximum of Solar Cycle 20, a major geomagnetic storm drove the Dst index to approximately −429 nT. The event occurred during the early satellite era when in-situ solar wind measurements were becoming available, providing a more complete picture of storm drivers than had been possible for earlier events. The storm caused significant HF radio disruptions, particularly on polar routes, and aurora was visible at mid-latitudes across North America and Europe. GIC effects were detected in power transmission infrastructure, though grid failures were not as severe as those that would occur in later, more infrastructure-dependent decades.
